item.title: Weird error on exit/logout when using Bash
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description:
Reproduced, debugged, found root cause. When you log in with bash, the name given to the shell is -bash (the trailing dash indicating that it’s a login shell). Some code called during the login process and potentially during the logout process as well runs command -v <name of calling executable> to determine the path to the running script. In this context, that runs command -v -bash. But because of the leading dash, bash attempts to parse -bash as a series of options (-b, -a, -s, -h), and because command doesn’t recognize a -b option, it gripes about it, and thus you see the error.

I think the solution is to run command -v -- <name of calling executable> instead. The -- will tell Bash that what follows should not be parsed as options.

item.title: Two of my laptop CPU cores are offline on Kicksecure
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description:
You’re most likely running into a consequence of hyperthreading being disabled in Kicksecure. Hyperthreading allows a single CPU core to “pretend” to be multiple cores; this provides greater performance in some situations, but also opens the door for entire families of CPU vulnerabilities like L1TF/Foreshadow. It is therefore recommended that you leave hyperthreading disabled and ignore the offline CPU “cores”.

If you want to enable hyperthreading anyway, you may be able to use the instructions here to add the smt=-1 parameter to your kernel command line:

Kicksecure – 13 May 26

Temporary Kernel Boot Parameter Change - grub bootloader Configuration Changes

Kernel Boot Parameter Changes

item.title: Calamares 3.3.14 segfault during manual partitioning (Lenovo Slim Pro X 14ARH7 / Ryzen 9 6900HS)
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description:
Some of the screens are missing which makes it a bit hard to tell what’s happening, but:

  1. Are you sure your system is actually a UEFI system? You probably already know this, but there are two major firmware types used by most PCs, BIOS (older) and UEFI (newer).
  2. If your previous OS install didn’t have an EFI system partition, you’re using a BIOS system, and should NOT create a UEFI partition at all. If your system does have an EFI partition, do NOT create a new one, instead tell Calamares to reuse the existing one without reformatting it.

That might resolve the problem.

If the issue really is that you can’t create new LUKS partitions alongside existing ones, then you may have to use the erase disk option. I somewhat doubt this is the issue though. Will try to reproduce.

item.title: Calamares 3.3.14 segfault during manual partitioning (Lenovo Slim Pro X 14ARH7 / Ryzen 9 6900HS)
item.dc:creator: @kicksecure.jr6xp
item.description:
@arraybolt3 used ai to do some troubleshooting.

could this be the issue and some solutions?? or s omething else?

The Calamares LUKS/partition-creation segfault — known, widespread, with workarounds

This class of bug isn’t limited to Kicksecure; it appears across distros that ship Calamares with the sfdisk backend, especially in manual partitioning + LUKS scenarios:

Upstream bug trackers:

  • Codeberg Calamares #2426 — “Segmentation fault while creating LUKS partitions” (the exact crash: installer dies at partition-creation job) → #2426 - Segmentation fault while creating LUKS partitions - Calamares/calamares - Codeberg.org
  • Codeberg Calamares #2454 — “Replace Partition” splits partitions incorrectly with separate /boot (Calamares forces a new /boot + LUKS split even when one exists; workaround: delete existing /boot and LUKS first) → #2454 - "Replace Partion" Issues with Separate /boot - Calamares/calamares - Codeberg.org

Reports on other distros (same backend, same symptom):

  • Manjaro: installer stops/crashes making a LUKS partition — Manjaro Installer Stops After Trying to Make a LUKS Partition - Support - Manjaro Linux Forum
  • Manjaro: Calamares crashes entering custom partitioning — Calamares crashes upon entering the custom disk partitioning section - Support - Manjaro Linux Forum
  • Manjaro: encryption partition bugs (formatting an existing LUKS/ext4 partition never offers the encrypt option) — Problem with calamares and partition encryption - Support - Manjaro Linux Forum
  • Nitrux: “fails to create new partitions” — Calamares fails to create new partitions when selecting 'Replace partition' · Issue #55 · Nitrux/nitrux-bug-tracker · GitHub

Workarounds people actually use successfully:

  1. Pre-create all partitions outside Calamares (parted/cryptsetup/mkfs from a live session or GParted), then in Calamares only assign mount points to existing partitions — the buggy create-partition job never runs. This is the most-cited reliable workaround across the threads above.
  2. Delete the pre-existing LUKS//boot partitions first, then use guided modes (“Replace a partition” / “Erase disk”) — guided paths bypass manual-mode bugs (per Codeberg #2454 and the Manjaro threads).
  3. Skip Calamares entirely — some users install the underlying distro via its non-Calamares installer (e.g., Debian’s debian-installer) or by-hand Arch-style, then use Kicksecure’s official Debian-morph path ( Install Kicksecure inside Debian ) to transform it into Kicksecure.
  4. Fresh-disk installs don’t hit it — the crash class is overwhelmingly “manual partitions + existing LUKS/dual-boot disk”; Erase Disk on an empty drive generally works.

Root cause area (for devs): the KPMCore pmsfdiskbackendplugin partition-creation path, and Calamares’s LUKS handling limitations (it also has documented weaknesses reusing existing LUKS partitions and separate /boot configurations, per the Calamares LUKS deployment wiki: Deploy LUKS · calamares/calamares Wiki · GitHub).

item.title: How to verify running Kicksecure version?
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description:
catharinewine25315:

—

There are hallmarks of generative AI use in this comment like the em-dash quoted. We allow the use of these technologies for writing forum posts, but require that use be disclosed up-front. Please see:

Kicksecure – 13 Sep 26

Kicksecure Policy on Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Do not post AI-generated content without clearly marking it as AI-generated.

catharinewine25315:

Still, a minor version in /etc/kicksecure_version has some diagnostic value even if it can’t prove you’re fully updated: it tells you which snapshot you actually booted, which helps when filing a bug report or comparing two machines.

“Snapshot” isn’t meaningful as Kicksecure doesn’t have a native snapshotting mechanism at the moment. Because package updates happen without point releases sometimes (frequently even), the only way to be sure what software versions you’re running are to check package versions directly using something like dpkg-query -s <package name>.

catharinewine25315:

An EOL warning would arguably be the more useful thing to surface.

EOL warnings are already integrated into Kicksecure.

Environment

  • ISO: Kicksecure-LXQt-18.2.4.2.Intel_AMD64.iso (OpenPGP-verified)

item.title: How to verify running Kicksecure version?
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description: I’m not sure how this could be done in a way that is particularly valuable. Knowing the build version you are effectively running might be useful to ensure you aren’t missing updates, but embedding the latest point release version into a package won’t do that, all it will do is tell you that you have a new enough version of that specific package installed. The best way to tell if you have all updates installed is to run systemcheck, which will tell you if you have Kicksecure repos enabled and if there are any updates available. If you have Kicksecure repos enabled and there are no updates available, then you have everything installed and don’t need to worry (unless of course you’re running an EOL major version of Kicksecure). I’m not sure what other use an updating build version number would have.

item.title: Emerg-shutdown not showing any messages at shutdown? (18.0.8.7 Feedback)
item.dc:creator: @spartack
item.description:
arraybolt3:

systemd tries to make sure everything it tracks is killed before issuing a reboot syscall. If a process is stuck in a kernel thread and won’t respond to even SIGKILL, it will simply hang forever waiting for it to respond. emerg-shutdown on the other hand just issues a reboot syscall when it decides the system should be shut down, triggering the kernel to cut power to the device regardless of what may or may not be hung.

It may be good to be documented in the docs, I tried but I think I have no permissions to modify that page.

As the options available security-misc/usr/src/security-misc/emerg-shutdown.c#security-misc-shared at 9535bf8e9c37bb65d1b4cabb39b7f6bc5ee9f29f · Kicksecure/security-misc · GitHub

Anyway, after reviewing the thread and the documentation I think I confused the use case of the variable ENSURE_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT=30 available in the configuration file /etc/security-misc/emerg-shutdown/30_security_misc.conf. Ensure shutdown will just trigger the kernel to cut the power without waiting any service to be closed, similar to unplug the computer from the grid, this is what I have understood from the documentation.

item.title: Emerg-shutdown not showing any messages at shutdown? (18.0.8.7 Feedback)
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description:
spartack:

If a service stuck the shutdown, how is the process to terminate it?

systemd tries to make sure everything it tracks is killed before issuing a reboot syscall. If a process is stuck in a kernel thread and won’t respond to even SIGKILL, it will simply hang forever waiting for it to respond. emerg-shutdown on the other hand just issues a reboot syscall when it decides the system should be shut down, triggering the kernel to cut power to the device regardless of what may or may not be hung.

spartack:

As I understand for the configuration file, systemd timeout will try to terminate the process before the emerg-shutdown timeout arrive, right?

Yes. Reducing the DefaultTimeoutStopSec will make systemd resort to force-killing everything during shutdown sooner than it would otherwise. If it manages to do that and get to issuing a reboot syscall before emerg-shutdown gets there, the kernel settings will wipe the RAM of killed processes during shutdown.

item.title: Emerg-shutdown not showing any messages at shutdown? (18.0.8.7 Feedback)
item.dc:creator: @spartack
item.description:
If a service stuck the shutdown, how is the process to terminate it?

As I understand for the configuration file, systemd timeout will try to terminate the process before the emerg-shutdown timeout arrive, right? That would run a normal (non forced) shutdown that would completely clean the RAM.

I don’t know exactly the seconds RAM decay take after powering off, but if you force a reboot it will clear the RAM automatically. We dodge the risk of a RAM dump after a power off.

## Enabling ensure-shutdown.service will cause shutdown to always
## take at least as long as systemd's DefaultTimeoutStopSec (which by default
## is 90 seconds). If you are going to enable ensure-shutdown.service, it is
## highly recommended to set DefaultTimeoutStopSec to a much smaller value,
## such as 5 seconds. The maximum shutdown time set here should be at least 10
## seconds *longer* than DefaultTimeoutStopSec, to give normal shutdown a
## chance to actually succeed before forcibly shutting down the system.
ENSURE_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT=30

item.title: Kicksecure 18: emerg-shutdown causes immediate power-off during boot after LUKS unlock
item.dc:creator: @SpecialBook
item.description:
# Kicksecure 18: emerg-shutdown causes immediate power-off during boot after LUKS unlock

Environment

  • OS: Kicksecure 18, bare metal, LXQt
  • Kernel: `6.12.113+deb13-amd64`
  • Package: `security-misc-shared 3:54.2-1`
  • Storage: Internal NVMe SSD
  • Root filesystem: ext4 on LUKS encryption
  • Initramfs: dracut
  • Hardware: Lenovo laptop, AMD platform

Problem

After entering the LUKS passphrase during a normal boot, the computer abruptly powers off before reaching the login screen.

The issue is reproducible whenever `emerg-shutdown.service` is enabled.

Booting with the following temporary kernel parameters allows the system to start normally:

```text
systemd.mask=emerg-shutdown.service rd.systemd.mask=emerg-shutdown.service
```

No shutdown reason or kernel panic is visible in the journal.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Enable `emerg-shutdown.service`.
  2. Reboot normally.
  3. Enter the LUKS passphrase.
  4. The system proceeds into normal systemd initialization.
  5. `emerg-shutdown.service` starts.
  6. The computer abruptly powers off.

Troubleshooting performed

**1. Recovery mode**

Booting into single-user recovery mode and then running `exit` allowed the system to continue booting successfully.

Booting directly into `multi-user.target` did not resolve the problem.

**2. Disabling emerg-shutdown**

Masking `emerg-shutdown.service` during boot prevents the unexpected power-off.

**4. Testing without boot-device monitoring**

Created a temporary systemd override replacing `ExecStart` with:

```ini
[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/bin/emerg-shutdown --keys=KEY_LEFTCTRL|KEY_RIGHTCTRL,KEY_LEFTALT|KEY_RIGHTALT,KEY_END
```

the system again powered off during boot.

This suggests that monitoring the NVMe device is not required to reproduce the issue. However, the binary still initializes and processes Netlink events even when `–devices` is omitted.

**5. NVMe and USBGuard**

The root-device detection helper correctly resolves the encrypted root filesystem to its underlying NVMe partition.

Available kernel logs show normal NVMe detection and filesystem mounting, without obvious device disconnection or I/O errors.

USBGuard logs show permitted devices and no obvious blocking event associated with the issue.

Relevant logs

From an unsuccessful boot:

```text
systemd[1]: Starting emerg-shutdown.service - Emergency shutdown when boot media is removed…
emerg-shutdown: path: /
emerg-shutdown: is block device: no
emerg-shutdown: path: /dev/mapper/[REDACTED_LUKS_DEVICE]
emerg-shutdown: is block device: yes
emerg-shutdown: real_dev_path: /dev/dm-0
emerg-shutdown: path: /dev/dm-0
emerg-shutdown: is block device: yes
emerg-shutdown: dm slaves_dir: /sys/class/block/dm-0/slaves
emerg-shutdown: path: /dev/nvme0n1p5
emerg-shutdown: is block device: yes
systemd[1]: Started emerg-shutdown.service - Emergency shutdown when boot media is removed.
```

In a separate failed boot with the keyboard-only override:

```text
systemd[1]: Started emerg-shutdown.service - Emergency shutdown when boot media is removed.
```

The system then powered off unexpectedly. No clear reason was recorded.

The journal excerpts are selected from different failed boots. Identifying values and timestamps have been removed.

Expected behavior

`emerg-shutdown` should remain enabled and permit normal system boot unless the configured emergency key combination is pressed or a monitored boot device is actually removed.

Questions

  1. Is this a known issue with `security-misc-shared 3:54.2-1`?
  2. Is there a recommended fix that preserves the emergency keyboard shortcut rather than disabling the service entirely?

I would prefer to keep the emergency shutdown functionality enabled.

Thank you.

item.title: Emerg-shutdown not showing any messages at shutdown? (18.0.8.7 Feedback)
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description: ram-wipe itself doesn’t really “run” anymore nowadays, instead kernel configuration is used so that RAM is wiped automatically on an as-possible basis. A normal shutdown probably will indeed result in more RAM contents being wiped, but this is mainly useful when the attacker isn’t physically close nearby while the system is fully powered on. If there is a significant chance of an attacker reaching the system before it is fully powered off, there is potentially quite a bit more recoverable data than if they reach the system after it is fully powered off but before RAM decay has fully taken effect (depending on what software, if any, decides to hang during shutdown).

item.title: Emerg-shutdown not showing any messages at shutdown? (18.0.8.7 Feedback)
item.dc:creator: @arraybolt3
item.description:
spartack:
  • emerg-shutdown.service

This is the autostart service for the “immediately shutdown on boot drive removal or panic key press” code.

spartack:
  • ensure-shutdown.service
  • ensure-shutdown-trigger.service

These are part of an optional feature that can be used to prevent a shutdown hang. It uses emerg-shutdown under the hood. The feature is implemented in a non-ideal way currently (it will actually increase shutdown time by default), so it’s disabled by default and will probably eventually be removed in favor of a better implementation. If you want to enable it anyway though, see:

github.com/Kicksecure/security-misc

etc/security-misc/emerg-shutdown/30_security_misc.conf%23security-misc-shared

master 
## Copyright (C) 2025 - 2025 ENCRYPTED SUPPORT LLC <adrelanos@whonix.org>
## See the file COPYING for copying conditions.

## Please use "/etc/security-misc/emerg-shutdown/50_user.conf" or
## "/usr/local/etc/security-misc/emerg-shutdown/50_user.conf"
## for your custom configuration, which will override the defaults found here.
## When Kicksecure is updated, this file may be overwritten.

## Set the key combo for forcing immediate shutdown. See the "Keys and
## buttons" section of "/usr/include/linux/input-event-codes.h" for possibly
## supported values. Not all keys are supported.
##
## All specified keys must be depressed at the same time to trigger a
## shutdown. Use a comma (",") to separate keys. If you want to alias certain
## keys to each other from emerg-shutdown's standpoint, use a pipe
## character("|").
##
## The default key sequence triggers a shutdown when Ctrl+Alt+Delete is
## pressed, allowing the use of either the left or right Ctrl and Alt keys.
EMERG_SHUTDOWN_KEYS="KEY_LEFTCTRL|KEY_RIGHTCTRL,KEY_LEFTALT|KEY_RIGHTALT,KEY_END"
